summary: We developed a child friendly video for kids to understand heavy and complex nasa data in easy format for children to learn it adress our challenges because our goal was to make actual nasa data accessible to everyone and easily understood for children. It is important because children who are interested in learning about space and nasa but have a hard time understanding them are now in easy format
details:
Our project is "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," a 3 minute 52 second animated story video, plus a 28-second demo, about robots NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. It tells the story of ALSEP, the Moon buggy, Viking, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, with InSight as the main hero. The video begins with a team card showing each member's name and role. It then explains, in simple words and animation, what each machine was, why it was sent, how it worked, why it stopped or stayed, and what it taught us. It has no narration. Everything is shown through captions, animated cards, counters, simple diagrams and music, so it works on a silent phone.
How it works: each scene shows one machine, with a short cartoon animation on the left and cards on the right. Counters show the numbers, such as 1,319 marsquakes and 83 sols against 7 planned days. Short "kid view" lines turn each fact into something children can picture. The video ends with the lessons and our student idea, ARES Scout. We clearly label ARES Scout as a concept, not a NASA vehicle. Our title line, "I was built to work. I was left behind. But my discoveries are still here," is marked as creative interpretation, not a NASA quote.
Benefits and impact: it helps children and students see left-behind equipment as records of discovery, not junk. It gives teachers a quick, accurate introduction to Moon and Mars exploration. It also shows how one weak link, such as dust or a lost relay, can end a mission, which is a useful lesson for future missions.
Tools: Claude (an AI assistant) helped organize our handwritten notes, draft the script and generate the animation and music. We rendered the video with Python, the Pillow and NumPy libraries, and FFmpeg. We used the DejaVu Sans font. We hosted the video on YouTube.
Creativity: we turn mission history into a story with a clear beginning, middle and end, pair robots with opposite endings (InSight silenced by dust, Sojourner outliving its plan), and make numbers visible.
Factors we considered: accuracy (we checked facts against NASA sources and left out anything we couldn't confirm), age-appropriate language, accessibility (captions on every scene, readable text), honest labeling (every frame carries an "SI-generated | Made with Claude" watermark, and the file's metadata says so too), and no use of NASA logos, patches or photos.
